### <a id="inf-memory-budget"></a>9. Estimate a serving memory budget for a 70-billion-parameter model, explicitly choosing precision, context and concurrency assumptions.

*Applied scenario · [Inference, serving and cost](../themes/inference-economics.md) · [Checklist](../themes/inference-economics.md#inf-memory-budget)*

I would state a hypothetical architecture before budgeting: 70 billion parameters, 80 layers, eight KV heads and head width 128. BF16 weights occupy about 140 GB, which is about 130 GiB; int8 roughly 70 GB and four-bit roughly 35 GB, excluding quantisation metadata. For BF16 KV, bytes equal 2 times concurrency times layers times tokens times KV heads times head width times two. Choosing 8,192 tokens and four concurrent sequences gives 10 GiB of KV cache. On two hypothetical 80 GiB accelerators, tensor parallelism could split weights and KV heads, leaving roughly 9.8 GiB per device for activations, buffers, fragmentation and headroom. I would verify actual usable memory and peak allocations, then lower concurrency if needed. This is a capacity estimate, not evidence that the configuration meets a latency SLO.

Read: [Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="inf-cost-reduction"></a>10. You are asked to reduce serving cost by an order of magnitude. Rank the levers and explain how you would test whether that target is achievable.

*Applied scenario · [Inference, serving and cost](../themes/inference-economics.md) · [Checklist](../themes/inference-economics.md#inf-cost-reduction)*

I'd rank levers by where the money goes, starting from a breakdown in cost per successful task at the required quality and latency SLO: input versus output tokens, the repeated share of input, and accelerator utilisation. Each output token needs its own decode step, so if output dominates, prompt caching barely helps; the levers are a smaller or distilled model for the traffic it can handle, and shorter answers. If long repeated prompts dominate, prefix caching and trimmed context come first. If utilisation is low, batching and right-sized capacity can beat any model change. Quantisation makes each step cheaper but removes no work, and its ceiling is a few-fold gain, not tenfold. Levers interact: a smaller model shrinks what caching and quantisation can still save, so multiplying separate gains overstates the total. I'd measure each lever alone, then prove the combined stack on replayed production traffic against the quality bar and p99. If cost is mostly output from a model that can't shrink without failing the bar, tenfold may not exist, and I'd say so upfront.

Read: [Optimizing inference](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/llm_optims) · [Site Reliability Engineering](https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="inf-tail-regression"></a>11. After a deployment, p99 latency doubles although model weights are unchanged. How do you isolate the cause?

*Applied scenario · [Inference, serving and cost](../themes/inference-economics.md) · [Checklist](../themes/inference-economics.md#inf-tail-regression)*

With weights unchanged I'd search around the model, starting with where slow requests spend their time: queue wait, prefill, decode and dependency calls, read from traces of tail requests before and after the release, because stage p99s don't add up to the end-to-end p99. Each component points somewhere different. Longer queueing means capacity fell or load rose: a lower batch limit, a missing replica or a new co-located workload pushes utilisation toward one, where waiting grows nonlinearly, so a small loss can double the tail. Longer prefill suggests a changed system prompt or template broke the shared prefix and collapsed the prefix-cache hit rate. Longer decode points to longer outputs or KV evictions forcing recomputation. Longer dependency time is a retrieval or tool tail. I'd also compare the traffic mix, since a new client brings longer prompts without any code change. Then one hypothesis at a time, confirmed by rollback or canary; a canary proves causality only under comparable traffic and neighbours, otherwise I'd replay recorded traffic against both versions.

Read: [The Tail at Scale](https://research.google/pubs/the-tail-at-scale/)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="rag-chunking"></a>12. Choose a chunking approach for technical documentation, including how you preserve meaning across section boundaries.

*Applied scenario · [RAG and retrieval](../themes/rag-retrieval.md) · [Checklist](../themes/rag-retrieval.md#rag-chunking)*

I'd split along the document's structure, because an embedding is one vector per chunk: a chunk that straddles two topics averages them and matches neither, and one cut mid-procedure loses what this flag or the step above refers to. The unit is a section; sections longer than a few hundred tokens split recursively at paragraphs with a small overlap, while code blocks and tables stay whole, a table keeping its header row. Each chunk carries its heading chain, document id and position, so it's intelligible away from its page and links back precisely. The trade-off is size: small chunks match precisely but lose context, large ones keep it but blur the vector and fill the prompt. My baseline is a fixed-size window with overlap, compared on representative questions with known source passages: recall at k for retrieval, then answer quality, with tables and answers spanning two sections checked separately. The boundary: this needs real structure, and on scanned PDFs or inconsistent headings I'd fall back to recursive size-based splitting.

Read: [Contextual Retrieval in AI Systems](https://www.anthropic.com/news/contextual-retrieval)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="rag-hybrid"></a>13. When would you combine lexical and dense retrieval, and how would you merge their rankings?

*Knowledge · [RAG and retrieval](../themes/rag-retrieval.md) · [Checklist](../themes/rag-retrieval.md#rag-hybrid)*

It's worth combining when queries contain both exact strings and free wording. Lexical search is irreplaceable for identifiers, error codes, function names, versions and rare terms that an embedding doesn't distinguish; dense search pulls in paraphrases and synonyms where there's no word overlap at all. You can't add their scores together directly: a lexical score isn't normalised and isn't comparable with cosine similarity. It's more practical to fuse by rank, for instance reciprocal rank fusion, or to normalise within a single query, or to take the union of candidates and rerank with a cross-encoder, at which point the original scales stop mattering entirely. I'd test on a fixed query set with labelled relevance, switching off each branch and the reranking in turn to see what each part contributes. The price is a second index, an extra latency stage and cost. If queries are homogeneous, hybrid adds complexity without a gain.

Read: [Contextual Retrieval in AI Systems](https://www.anthropic.com/news/contextual-retrieval)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="rag-stage-evaluation"></a>14. How would you separately evaluate document retrieval and answer generation in a RAG application?

*Applied scenario · [RAG and retrieval](../themes/rag-retrieval.md) · [Checklist](../themes/rag-retrieval.md#rag-stage-evaluation)*

For representative questions I label answer-bearing passages and define acceptable answers separately. Retrieval is then measured by its own metrics, whether the needed passage appeared in the results and at what rank, and generation by groundedness, whether every statement rests on the context it was given, and by factual correctness. The key move is running generation with the gold passages as input: if the answer is right with them, retrieval or context assembly needs investigation; if not, the problem is the model, the prompt or the context format. Without that split, an end to end metric mixes two different defects and the team fixes the wrong stage. I'd keep the set small but alive, topping it up with real production failures. Limits: relevance labelling is subjective, gold passages don't reproduce the noise of real retrieval, and a judge model itself needs checking against human agreement.

Read: [Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401) · [Demystifying evals for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="rag-permissions"></a>15. Design retrieval that enforces the source system's access rights, including permission changes and shared caches.

*System design · [RAG and retrieval](../themes/rag-retrieval.md) · [Checklist](../themes/rag-retrieval.md#rag-permissions)*

The source system defines document permissions; retrieval must enforce them before content reaches the model. I pass the user's identity into search and filter candidates by access, then check authoritative permissions if indexed ACL freshness cannot be established. Post-filtering can damage recall, and applying controls only after generation is too late. Permission changes and deletions need measurable propagation, revoked grants must invalidate caches, and cached answers must respect the current caller's access. A shared embedding cache need not be per user if it cannot expose restricted content and retrieval remains authorised. I test revoked access, deleted documents and users without rights, including citations, suggestions and logs. Stale content can be labelled; uncertain authorisation must fail closed rather than merely display a warning.

Read: [Document-level access control](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/search-document-level-access-overview)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="rag-ann-index"></a>16. Compare exact search, HNSW and IVF-PQ for an embedding index under memory, recall and latency constraints.

*Knowledge · [RAG and retrieval](../themes/rag-retrieval.md) · [Checklist](../themes/rag-retrieval.md#rag-ann-index)*

I'd start with exact search over a sample of queries: it gives the baseline against which the word recall means anything at all. HNSW builds a multi layer graph of neighbours and descends it greedily: search is fast and accurate and inserts need no retraining, but deletes are usually only marked, and the graph lives entirely in memory and costs dearly there. IVF-PQ first divides the space into coarse clusters and looks at only the nearest few, storing vectors compressed by product quantisers: it cuts memory by an order of magnitude or more, but quantisation itself loses accuracy and the clustering has to be trained on representative data. I'd choose by measuring recall against the exact baseline at the target latency, and separately measure memory footprint, the cost of updates and deletions, and behaviour under metadata filters. A small collection needs no approximate index at all, and no index will fix bad embeddings.

Read: [Efficient and robust approximate nearest neighbor search using Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.09320) · [Faiss indexes](https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/wiki/Faiss-indexes)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="agt-react"></a>17. What does interleaving reasoning with tool observations add to a language-model agent compared with reasoning alone?

*Knowledge · [Agents, tools and protocols](../themes/agents-tools.md) · [Checklist](../themes/agents-tools.md#agt-react)*

Reasoning alone can't check its own premises: if the model assumes a wrong fact in step two, every later step builds on it, and the chain gets more fluent, not more correct. Interleaving adds the one channel that can contradict the model. It states a thought, takes an action, and the observation that comes back, not the plan, decides the next step, so an empty search or an unexpected value forces a revision before the final answer. The reasoning, in turn, tracks progress and chooses the next action, which acting alone lacks. The cost is latency, another model call and more context per round, plus tool errors, empty results and junk the model must not mistake for fact. I'd run the same tasks three ways, reasoning only, acting only and interleaved, and compare success rate, cost per task and how often the agent recovers after a failed call. The boundary: when the model already knows the answer, uninformative results can derail it, and a silently wrong tool makes it confidently wrong.

Read: [ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="agt-retries"></a>18. Design recovery from tool errors and timeouts, including cases where a timed-out call may already have changed external state.

*System design · [Agents, tools and protocols](../themes/agents-tools.md) · [Checklist](../themes/agents-tools.md#agt-retries)*

Before retrying, I classify the outcome: transient failure, permanent failure or ambiguous completion. A timeout on a write is ambiguous because the operation may still be running or already committed. For writes, I persist a client-generated idempotency key with the task and reuse it under the provider's documented guarantees. Without that guarantee, a state read alone is insufficient: it may be stale while the original operation remains in flight. I require an authoritative terminal outcome or reconciliation; otherwise I stop automated retries. Safe retries have an attempt budget, overall deadline and exponential backoff with jitter. When that budget expires, I escalate with the operation history and unresolved status. Idempotency depends on provider semantics, retention and key scope; merely attaching a key does not make a write safe.

Read: [Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency](https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="agt-tool-surface"></a>19. How would you select, name and document tools so that a model chooses the right operation and arguments?

*System design · [Agents, tools and protocols](../themes/agents-tools.md) · [Checklist](../themes/agents-tools.md#agt-tool-surface)*

The model chooses a tool only from its name, description and schema, so every pair of overlapping tools is a decision it can get wrong, and every free-text argument is a place to invent a value. I'd shape tools around the agent's tasks, not the API's endpoints: a search instead of a list that dumps every record, names prefixed by service, enumerations wherever options are finite, and a strict schema so validation rejects a bad argument before the downstream system sees it. The real trade-off is granularity: a few high-level tools cut selection errors but make arguments complex, while many thin ones keep arguments simple but make selection ambiguous and chains longer. Results are paginated and capped, and an error says what to change. On a fixed set of realistic tasks I'd measure the share of calls with the right tool and valid arguments and the tokens per task, before and after each merge or rename. The boundary: once the set grows into dozens of tools, selection degrades even with good descriptions, so I'd load tools per task.

Read: [Writing effective tools for AI agents—using AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="agt-termination"></a>20. Define completion and stopping conditions for an agent loop so it cannot spend indefinitely on an unfinished task.

*System design · [Agents, tools and protocols](../themes/agents-tools.md) · [Checklist](../themes/agents-tools.md#agt-termination)*

The loop has to end in an explicit terminal state, and there are several: success, blocked, cancelled by the user, and budget exhausted. They cannot be merged, because the response differs: success closes the task, blocked needs a human, and budget exhausted says honestly that we never learned whether the task was doable. I define progress from observable state in the environment, not from the model's confidence, and alongside it I keep hard limits on steps, money and time; without them an agent will cycle through options forever on an unsolvable task. The cost is obvious: some genuinely long tasks get cut off, so on stopping you save state, what was done and which side effects are already applied, so a resume or handoff does not repeat them. The limit: budgets bound spend, not quality, and an agent can stop on time with a formally complete but useless result.

Read: [Building Effective AI Agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="agt-approval"></a>21. Design human approval for consequential agent actions, including how approval remains bound to the exact action being executed.

*System design · [Agents, tools and protocols](../themes/agents-tools.md) · [Checklist](../themes/agents-tools.md#agt-approval)*

Approval works only if the person sees the concrete action, not the intent: recipient, amount, object and how reversible the consequences are, exactly as they will go to the external system. So permission binds not to the conversation or the session but to the validated arguments of one specific call: we freeze them, show them, and at execution recheck the initiator's rights and that fields are unchanged. If the model changed even one material argument after approval, the old permission is void and a new one is requested. I make execution idempotent so a retry after a network failure is not a second charge, and I log the decision, its author, time and result. The limit: this protects against mistaken and externally prompted actions, but under a stream of requests it degenerates into a formality: people approve without looking, so only actions whose cost of error is real deserve it.

Read: [Building Effective AI Agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents) · [Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency](https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="pt-rlhf"></a>22. Walk through a preference-based RLHF pipeline and explain the roles of the reward model and reference-policy penalty.

*Knowledge · [Fine-tuning and post-training](../themes/post-training.md) · [Checklist](../themes/post-training.md#pt-rlhf)*

RLHF splits into three stages that differ by data. First demonstrations: examples of desired answers, on which the base model is finetuned with supervised learning. Then preference pairs: a person sees several answers to one prompt and ranks them, and on those comparisons you train a reward model, a separate model predicting which answer a person picks. In the third stage the policy is optimised against that reward on its own rollouts, with a penalty for diverging from the reference model added to the objective, usually a KL divergence; without it the policy drifts to where reward is high and the text has degraded. That is the trade-off: push harder on reward and you reach its overoptimisation sooner. Check on held-out human preferences, not on the reward itself, and watch how divergence from the reference tracks the real gain. The reward model inherits annotator bias, and optimisation amplifies it.

Read: [Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="pt-dpo"></a>23. Compare DPO with PPO-based RLHF, including the assumptions behind offline preference learning and reasons to collect fresh rollouts.

*Knowledge · [Fine-tuning and post-training](../themes/post-training.md) · [Checklist](../themes/post-training.md#pt-dpo)*

DPO starts from the same KL-regularised objective as PPO-based RLHF but uses its closed-form optimum: the reward becomes implicit, β times the log ratio of policy to reference probability, plus a term depending only on the prompt. In the Bradley–Terry preference model that term cancels, so the loss is written directly on the policy: a logistic loss on β times the gap between chosen and rejected log ratios. β plays the KL penalty's role, and there's no reward model, value network or sampling loop. The price is an assumption: fixed pairs must cover what the policy will generate, since the loss shapes only responses in pairs and can lower the likelihood of both answers or drift toward length. PPO scores fresh rollouts from the current policy, catching errors where they occur, at the cost of a reward model that can be exploited. I'd compare held-out win rate against the reference, KL and length drift. A simpler loss isn't better alignment: when the change needed is large or the reward is verifiable, fresh rollouts earn their cost.

Read: [Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="pt-lora"></a>24. Derive the low-rank weight update used by LoRA and propose an experiment for choosing its rank.

*Knowledge · [Fine-tuning and post-training](../themes/post-training.md) · [Checklist](../themes/post-training.md#pt-lora)*

LoRA freezes the original weight matrix and trains a low-rank correction instead: ΔW = BA, where B is d by r, A is r by k, and r is much smaller than both d and k. Instead of d times k trainable parameters you are left with r times the sum of d and k, orders of magnitude fewer at small rank, and at inference the correction can be merged into the base weights with no extra latency. The constraint is that rank sets capacity: too small an r simply can't hold the behaviour change you need. The experiment is straightforward. Fix the data and the set of target modules, vary only r over a grid, and compare quality on held-out tasks while checking for regressions in general capability. Merging the adapter is convenient, but it gives up keeping several adapters on one base and switching them per request.

Read: [LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="pt-qlora"></a>25. How does QLoRA reduce finetuning memory, and which tensors remain trainable or require higher precision?

*Knowledge · [Fine-tuning and post-training](../themes/post-training.md) · [Checklist](../themes/post-training.md#pt-qlora)*

QLoRA saves memory by keeping base weights quantised to four bits and frozen while only low-rank adapters, kept in 16-bit, are trained: gradients flow back through the dequantised base weights, but weight gradients and optimiser states exist for the adapters alone, and those were exactly what ate most of the memory in full finetuning. Three mechanisms work together: NF4, a quantisation format designed for normally distributed weights; double quantisation, which compresses the quantisation constants themselves; and paged optimisers, which move optimiser states into host memory during spikes. You pay in compute, because weights are dequantised to the compute precision on every matrix multiply, which can slow training depending on implementation. Activation memory does not go anywhere and grows with sequence length and batch size, so on long context it becomes the binding constraint again. The limit: this is a way to fit finetuning into less memory, not a way to guarantee full-finetuning quality on any task.

Read: [QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14314)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="pt-method-choice"></a>26. Choose between prompt changes, retrieval and finetuning for a failing AI feature; include data freshness, latency and total cost.

*Applied scenario · [Fine-tuning and post-training](../themes/post-training.md) · [Checklist](../themes/post-training.md#pt-method-choice)*

I'd let a diagnostic pick the intervention: rerun a sample of real failures with the right document pasted into the prompt. If they now succeed, the model lacked knowledge, and retrieval fits: facts stay fresh without retraining and answers can cite sources, paid for with a search hop in latency and an index to keep current. If they still fail with the evidence in front of the model, it's instructions or behaviour, so I tighten the prompt with explicit rules and examples; that's cheap and becomes the baseline everything else must beat. Finetuning is for what persists after that, a format, tone or decision pattern the prompt can't hold reliably, once I have enough representative examples to train and still hold some out. Its cost is the lifecycle: labelling, training, evaluation and redoing it when the base model changes, though shorter prompts can cut per-request tokens and latency. I'd compare the options on one held-out set by cost per successful task. Finetuning won't keep facts fresh, and retrieval can't fix a model that ignores what it found.

Read: [Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401) · [LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="eval-judge"></a>27. Design an LLM judge and a calibration process that exposes order, verbosity and self-preference biases.

*System design · [Evaluation and observability](../themes/evals-observability.md) · [Checklist](../themes/evals-observability.md#eval-judge)*

A judge starts not with a prompt but with criteria: what counts as a good answer in this task, written so that two people would agree. Then you need a held-out calibration set with human labels; it measures the judge itself, otherwise we are simply trusting a model to grade a model. The known biases are checked by experiment: run each pair in both orders and see whether the verdict flips; pad answers with repetition that adds no content and see whether they start winning, to catch a reward for verbosity; compare how often the judge prefers its own family's answers with how often people do on the same pairs, since a judge can favour its own style even when authorship is hidden. I would track agreement between judge and people, the share of pairs where swapping order changes the decision, and send unreliable cases to experts. The limit: a judge measures conformance to criteria, not usefulness to the user, and wherever an answer can be checked deterministically an ordinary check is cheaper.

Read: [Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="eval-release-gate"></a>28. Design a release gate for prompt and model updates, including what happens when aggregate gains hide a critical regression.

*System design · [Evaluation and observability](../themes/evals-observability.md) · [Checklist](../themes/evals-observability.md#eval-release-gate)*

I'd version everything, prompt, model and parameters, dataset and grader code, and compare the candidate with a pinned baseline on the same items. The rule isn't one average: the aggregate must not drop, and each critical slice, safety, money, rare but expensive cases, has its own rule. The hard part is statistics on small slices. With 50 items at a 90 percent pass rate, the 95 percent interval is about plus or minus eight points, so a three-point regression is invisible. So I compare paired, item by item, with several samples per item, and count items that flipped from pass to fail; for the most severe failures I keep must-pass items where any flip blocks. Thresholds and severity weights are fixed before the run, because a strict gate rejects good releases and a loose one ships regressions, and that trade is a product decision. Then a canary on a small share of traffic with numeric rollback triggers. The boundary: the gate only sees failure modes the dataset covers.

Read: [Demystifying evals for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="eval-benchmark-mismatch"></a>29. Benchmark results improve but users report a worse product. What hypotheses would you test first?

*Applied scenario · [Evaluation and observability](../themes/evals-observability.md) · [Checklist](../themes/evals-observability.md#eval-benchmark-mismatch)*

I'd order the hypotheses by how cheaply each can be ruled out. First, causes outside the model: latency, answer format, truncation or a changed system prompt, visible in logs within a day. Second, a mix mismatch: classify a sample of live traffic by task type, language and length, and re-weight the benchmark gain by that mix; if the gain vanishes, the model improved where users aren't. Third, a regression on a slice the average hides, from per-slice deltas. Fourth, the direct test of the complaint: a blind side-by-side of the old and new model on sampled production prompts, judged by people or by a judge calibrated against them. If the new model wins there, the complaints are about something else, often changed expectations. Fifth, contamination: n-gram overlap with training data, and reworded benchmark items, where a real gain survives rewording. Reproduced complaints become test cases, but I'd hold part of them out, because optimising straight at them detaches the metric from usefulness again.

Read: [Rules of Machine Learning](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="eval-traces"></a>30. Design observability for a production LLM workflow: which spans, versions, costs and feedback should be linked?

*System design · [Evaluation and observability](../themes/evals-observability.md) · [Checklist](../themes/evals-observability.md#eval-traces)*

Every user task gets one trace id that all spans attach to, model calls, retrieval and tool calls, each tagged with the prompt, model, index and code versions, so a trace answers not only what broke but which change broke it. Each span records latency, tokens, cost, outcome and error code, and user feedback carries the same id. Content is the sensitive part, so structure and metrics are kept for every task, while full payloads are kept by tail-based sampling: every failed task, low judge score or thumbs-down, plus a small fixed share of successes as a baseline, with masked fields and short retention. Then a failure reads directly: a retrieval span that returned nothing followed by a confident answer goes into an ungrounded-answer bucket, not a model bucket. I'd measure the share of failures attributed to a stage, time to diagnose and payloads that escaped masking, and recurring buckets become eval cases. The boundary: a wrong but fluent answer looks like a success, so its payload survives only if feedback or a judge flags it.

Read: [Site Reliability Engineering](https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/) · [Demystifying evals for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="eval-agent-outcomes"></a>31. How should evaluation of a tool-using agent differ from grading one generated response?

*System design · [Evaluation and observability](../themes/evals-observability.md) · [Checklist](../themes/evals-observability.md#eval-agent-outcomes)*

The main difference: an agent has a result in the environment, and that is what you check, not the text in which it reported success. Saying it is done costs nothing, so evaluation reads the final state: was the record created, was the mail sent, what status is the ticket in. The second dimension is the trajectory: a task can be completed at the cost of extra calls, wasted money, or a dangerous action like deletion, and that is graded separately from completion, otherwise a bad path is masked by a good outcome. The third is repeatability: one lucky run proves nothing; you need several trials from the same clean environment state and a measured success rate, because the agent is non-deterministic. The limit: all this needs isolated environments with reproducible state; they are expensive and always poorer than reality, so some failure modes appear only in production.

Read: [Demystifying evals for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="mm-visual-input"></a>32. Compare projection layers, cross-attention and token-based integration for giving a language model access to images.

*Knowledge · [Multimodal and voice](../themes/multimodal-voice.md) · [Checklist](../themes/multimodal-voice.md#mm-visual-input)*

I'd separate the encoder that turns pixels into features from the interface that fuses them with the language model; the three options differ in the interface. A projection maps each patch feature into the model's embedding space, and the results sit in the sequence like text: cheap to train, decoder unchanged, but tokens scale with resolution, and a 336 × 336 image at 14-pixel patches is 576 tokens of context, prefill and KV cache. Cross-attention, as in Flamingo, keeps features outside the sequence, compresses them to a fixed set of vectors and inserts gated cross-attention layers into a frozen model, gates starting at zero so text behaviour is initially untouched; the sequence stays short, but new layers need training. Discrete tokens quantise the image into a learned codebook added to the vocabulary, so the model can also generate images, but quantisation loses fine detail. All three need alignment training on image-text pairs. I'd compare them on text-in-image and spatial tasks, plotting accuracy against visual tokens per image: on dense documents, fixed compression drops exactly what matters.

Read: [Flamingo: a Visual Language Model for Few-Shot Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.14198)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="mm-accents"></a>33. How would you improve and evaluate speech recognition for mixed-language utterances and different accents?

*Applied scenario · [Multimodal and voice](../themes/multimodal-voice.md) · [Checklist](../themes/multimodal-voice.md#mm-accents)*

I'd start with evaluation, because an average WER hides exactly the groups this work is for. I'd build slices by language, accent, noise and code-switching, each with enough distinct speakers, and report WER per slice with confidence intervals bootstrapped over speakers, since one speaker's utterances are correlated. Code-switching needs its own care: a model like Whisper predicts one language token per segment and decodes conditioned on it, so a switched phrase can come out transliterated or even translated, and scoring is ambiguous too, because a loanword written in the other script counts as an error unless normalisation rules settle it. Beside WER I'd track errors in names, amounts and other entities an action depends on, since one wrong digit outweighs many small slips. The cheap lever is biasing decoding with a term list or prompt, which helps only known words; fine-tuning on accented and code-switched audio reaches further but can regress other languages. I'd validate any adaptation on held-out speakers and domains, and treat a slice with only a few speakers as no evidence either way.

Read: [Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.04356)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="sd-enterprise-rag"></a>34. Design a knowledge assistant over ten million enterprise documents with per-user permissions and a continuously changing corpus.

*System design · [AI system design](../themes/ai-system-design.md) · [Checklist](../themes/ai-system-design.md#sd-enterprise-rag)*

I'd pin down query volume, freshness and permission semantics, then size. At an assumed twenty chunks per document that's two hundred million vectors, about 800 GB as 1,024-dimensional float32, so the index is sharded or product-quantised, with recall checked against exact search. Ingestion is event-driven: changed documents are re-chunked and re-embedded, deletions tombstoned at once, behind a versioned index. The decisive point is that permissions must propagate faster than reindexing. ACLs live on each chunk as group ids, updated without re-embedding, and the user's groups are resolved at query time, so a membership change applies on the next query. The filter belongs inside the ANN query: post-filtering a top-k can leave almost nothing for a user who sees a small slice of the corpus, while filtering during graph search keeps recall until the allowed set gets tiny, where I switch to exact search over that subset. I'd measure revocation lag at p99, filtered recall and answer grounding, and show a shard outage as partial coverage. Stale text can be shown with its date; uncertain authorisation fails closed.

Read: [Document-level access control](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/search/search-document-level-access-overview) · [Contextual Retrieval in AI Systems](https://www.anthropic.com/news/contextual-retrieval)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="sd-gateway"></a>35. Design an LLM gateway with provider routing, failover, caching, rate limits and enforceable spending budgets.

*System design · [AI system design](../themes/ai-system-design.md) · [Checklist](../themes/ai-system-design.md#sd-gateway)*

A gateway exists for one contract over different providers, so first I describe their capabilities, streaming output, tool calling, context limits, behaviour on failure, and unify only genuinely compatible semantics; the rest I expose explicitly rather than emulate, otherwise the client quietly gets different behaviour. Quotas and budgets I check before dispatch, per client, and they must account for retries, or failover eats the budget itself; when a budget is exhausted I return a clear error saying when to try again. I cache whole responses only where returning the same answer twice is acceptable, and the key includes the client, the model and its parameters, otherwise the cache serves another client's or another model's answer. The subtlest part is the failover boundary: once part of a response has gone to the client you cannot switch providers without breaking the stream, and a side-effecting call cannot be repeated without idempotency. The limit: a gateway levels interfaces and failures, but not the quality gap between models.

Read: [Scaling your API with rate limiters](https://stripe.com/blog/rate-limiters) · [Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency](https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="sd-support-agent"></a>36. Design a customer-support agent that can execute service actions and transfer the case to a human when needed.

*System design · [AI system design](../themes/ai-system-design.md) · [Checklist](../themes/ai-system-design.md#sd-support-agent)*

I'd make authority a property of the tools, not of the prompt. Each supported intent maps to a tool whose backend enforces the limits: the agent reads order status freely, issues a refund only below a threshold and only to the verified customer, and anything else isn't callable at all. Duplicates are prevented by the case record, not the model's memory: each action is written there as an intent with an idempotency key and a status before it executes, and the agent reads the record before acting, so a retry or a resumed conversation can't refund twice. Escalation triggers are observable: the customer asks for a person, the request is out of scope, a tool returned an ambiguous outcome, or the same issue comes back. The handoff carries the history, the actions and their results. I'd compare against human-only handling on resolution without a human, wrong-action rate, repeat contacts and escalation precision. The real boundary is the threshold: lower it and more cases escalate, raise it and the agent's mistakes become direct losses.

Read: [Building Effective AI Agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents) · [Writing effective tools for AI agents—using AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="sd-consumer-chat"></a>37. Design a streaming chat service for hundreds of millions of users, including capacity, conversation storage and graceful overload behaviour.

*System design · [AI system design](../themes/ai-system-design.md) · [Checklist](../themes/ai-system-design.md#sd-consumer-chat)*

KV-cache memory, not compute, caps concurrent streams, so I'd size from that. Suppose 100 million daily users, ten replies each, 20 seconds of streaming per reply: about 230,000 concurrent streams on average, say half a million at peak. A 70B-class model with 80 layers and eight 128-wide KV heads needs a third of a megabyte of bf16 cache per token, so a 4,000-token conversation holds 1.3 GB, and an assumed 80 GB of free cache per replica fits about 60 streams, far too few to saturate compute. That's roughly 8,000 replicas before headroom. So admission counts free cache blocks: a request starts only when its expected length fits, otherwise it waits in a bounded queue or is rejected at once with a retry hint. A closed connection cancels generation and frees its blocks. Conversations, two billion messages a day, go to an append-only store partitioned by conversation, so a dropped stream resumes from the last saved message. The boundary: with short chats or a quantised cache, decode throughput becomes the limit and admission counts tokens per step.

Read: [Site Reliability Engineering](https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/) · [Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="code-causal-attention"></a>38. Implement scaled dot-product attention with a causal mask and tests that would expose attention to future tokens.

*Coding · [Practical coding](../themes/coding-practical.md) · [Checklist](../themes/coding-practical.md#code-causal-attention)*

I'd start with an explicit contract on dimensions: batch, heads, length, head width, with a shape check at the entry, because most bugs here are swapped axes and silent broadcasting. Then scores as Q times K transposed on the last axis, division by the square root of head width, minus infinity at future positions j &gt; i, allowing the diagonal and past, a stable softmax that subtracts the row maximum, and multiplication by V. The mask has to come before softmax: zeroing the weights after normalisation is wrong, the sum is spoiled by future positions. I'd write two kinds of test: a tiny example with numbers worked out by hand, and a causality test that changes tokens after a position and confirms the outputs before it didn't move. A causal mask alone never empties a row, since the diagonal is allowed, but with a padding mask a row can be fully masked and softmax gives NaN, so I'd test that case. This is a teaching implementation: no memory saving like flash attention, and no inference caching.

Read: [Attention Is All You Need](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="code-token-bucket"></a>39. Implement a token-bucket limiter and explain what must change when several workers enforce the same limit.

*Coding · [Practical coding](../themes/coding-practical.md) · [Checklist](../themes/coding-practical.md#code-token-bucket)*

The bucket stores a token count and last refill time. On each call I measure elapsed time on a monotonic clock, add elapsed time times the refill rate, clip at capacity, and deduct what was asked for if there's enough. Capacity sets the burst you allow and the rate sets the average pace, the main trade-off. Avoid wall-clock time: a clock change or a sync will give a negative interval or hand out a full bucket. Check and deduct must be one atomic operation under a lock, otherwise two threads see the same last token. I'd test a burst on a full bucket, refusal on an empty one, and recovery after the right interval, injecting a fake clock instead of waiting. A shared limit across workers needs an external counter with a script that refills and deducts atomically, or the quota split per worker: cheaper, less exact at the boundaries.

Read: [Scaling your API with rate limiters](https://stripe.com/blog/rate-limiters)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="code-async-batches"></a>40. Write an asynchronous API batch processor with bounded concurrency, retry jitter and isolated per-item failures.

*Coding · [Practical coding](../themes/coding-practical.md) · [Checklist](../themes/coding-practical.md#code-async-batches)*

I'd use a fixed pool of workers pulling from a queue, not one task per item behind a semaphore, so a million items don't mean a million pending tasks. Each item runs in a wrapper that turns its own failures into a result, value, permanent error or cancelled, stored by input index, so one failure can't sink its siblings, unlike a task group that cancels everything on the first error. Each attempt has a timeout inside an overall deadline, and cancelling the batch cancels in-flight requests too, so the wrapper mustn't swallow cancellation. I retry only timeouts, connection errors, rate-limit responses and server errors, with capped exponential backoff and full jitter, a uniform random sleep up to the current backoff, so clients don't retry in waves, and a Retry-After header wins. Unsafe writes retry only with an idempotency key. Tests use a fake clock and API: partial success, a permanent error, the deadline firing mid-retry and cancellation halfway. The boundary: per-item backoff doesn't bound the aggregate rate, so against a shared quota I'd put a token bucket in front.

Read: [Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency](https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency) · [Site Reliability Engineering](https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="llm-experts"></a>41. How does sparse expert routing increase parameter capacity, and what costs remain despite activating only some experts?

*Knowledge · [LLM fundamentals](../themes/llm-fundamentals.md) · [Checklist](../themes/llm-fundamentals.md#llm-experts)*

Routing buys capacity, not free scale: the model holds far more parameters while any one token is computed by only a few of them. A router scores experts per token and sends it to the top few, so arithmetic grows with the experts activated rather than the total, and quality improves as experts specialise. Memory does not shrink: every expert's weights stay resident, and in distributed serving tokens travel to the device holding their expert, putting an all-to-all exchange on the critical path. I would measure tokens per expert to expose imbalance, the share dropped when an expert hits its capacity limit, and the all-to-all share of step time, judging quality against a dense model of the same active size. The argument holds only while routing stays balanced and batches are large enough to amortise that exchange.

Read: [Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="llm-latent-attention"></a>42. Explain how latent attention compresses the KV representation and what must be reconstructed at inference.

*Knowledge · [LLM fundamentals](../themes/llm-fundamentals.md) · [Checklist](../themes/llm-fundamentals.md#llm-latent-attention)*

Latent attention changes what you store, not how precisely you store it. Keys and values are projected down to a single low-rank latent vector per token, and that latent is what the cache holds; during attention it is projected back up to per-head keys and values, or the up-projections are folded into the query and output projections so attention runs on the latent directly, with the positional part cached as a small separate key. Cache bytes per token therefore fall by about the compression ratio, paid for with extra arithmetic on every decode step and more intricate kernels. I would measure cache bytes per token, the context length and batch size reachable within the same memory, decode throughput, and quality against a grouped-query baseline at an equal cache budget. The distinction matters because quantisation lowers the precision of the same tensors: the two compose, so each needs its own baseline or one saving gets counted twice. The gain is real only when the KV cache, not the weights, is what bounds you.

Read: [DeepSeek-V2: A Strong, Economical, and Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Language Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.04434)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="inf-prefix-cache"></a>43. What makes a prompt prefix reusable, and which changes invalidate or reduce the value of a prefix cache?

*Knowledge · [Inference, serving and cost](../themes/inference-economics.md) · [Checklist](../themes/inference-economics.md#inf-prefix-cache)*

Reuse is exact and token-level, not semantic: the cache holds attention state for a prefix, and a request reuses it only while its tokens match from position zero under the same model version, precision and parallel layout. One changed character near the start invalidates everything after it, which dictates prompt layout — system rules, tool definitions and long documents first; the user turn, timestamps, retrieved snippets and per-request identifiers last. Cache memory competes with the KV cache of live requests, and entries expire, so I would measure hit rate, the share of prefill tokens served from cache, time to first token with and without it, and cost per request. Two limits: caching removes prefill work only, so a short-prompt long-answer workload gains almost nothing, and entries must be scoped per tenant, because a shared cache turns time to first token into a side channel: a fast response confirms that someone else sent the same prefix, which lets an attacker test guesses about another tenant's prompt.

Read: [Prompt caching](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="inf-paged-cache"></a>44. How does paging the KV cache reduce waste, and what remains for the scheduler to solve?

*Knowledge · [Inference, serving and cost](../themes/inference-economics.md) · [Checklist](../themes/inference-economics.md#inf-paged-cache)*

Paging attacks fragmentation, not scarcity. If each request reserves one contiguous span sized for the longest answer it might produce, most of that reservation sits idle, and the free memory left over is unusable because it is scattered, so concurrency collapses well before the device is full. Paging stores the cache in fixed-size blocks with a per-request table mapping logical positions to physical blocks, so growth is incremental, internal waste is bounded by one partly filled block, and identical prefixes or parallel samples can point at shared blocks copied only on write. What it leaves untouched is policy: who is admitted when blocks run out, whose blocks are evicted or recomputed, and how long a request may wait. I would measure achieved batch size, the share of memory actually holding live tokens, preemption rate and p99 latency — paging widens the pipe, and a poor scheduler can still starve requests.

Read: [Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="inf-reasoning-budget"></a>45. A service can spend more on one reasoning run or generate several candidates and verify them. How would you allocate compute under a latency deadline?

*Applied scenario · [Inference, serving and cost](../themes/inference-economics.md) · [Checklist](../themes/inference-economics.md#inf-reasoning-budget)*

I would treat this as an empirical allocation question, not a preference. On the same held-out tasks I would run one long reasoning pass and a sample-and-verify strategy at several budgets, then compare success per unit of spend and per unit of wall-clock time, counting the verifier's own tokens and latency as part of the cost: a verifier that doubles latency can lose on a deadline it would win on cost. Sampling parallelises, so it often fits a deadline that a single long pass misses, but it only helps when a cheap check can tell candidates apart; without that, extra candidates add spend and no accuracy. Because the gain varies with difficulty, small where one pass already succeeds or nothing does and largest in between, I would route by an observable feature available before the answer exists, never by correctness. Then a hard token and time ceiling with a defined fallback, reporting spend per successful task and deadline misses. Where no strategy succeeds at any budget, extra test-time compute is wasted and a stronger model is the lever.

Read: [Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.03314) · [Evaluation best practices](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/evaluation-best-practices)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="rag-reranking"></a>46. Where should a cross-encoder reranker sit in a retrieval pipeline, and when does its quality gain justify latency?

*Knowledge · [RAG and retrieval](../themes/rag-retrieval.md) · [Checklist](../themes/rag-retrieval.md#rag-reranking)*

A cross-encoder belongs after a cheap retriever and before generation, scoring query-document pairs for a shortlist rather than the corpus: it reads the query and passage together, which is what makes it more accurate than comparing two independent embeddings, and also what makes it too slow to run over everything. The pipeline's ceiling is therefore the first stage's recall — a reranker cannot promote a document that was never fetched, so I measure recall at the candidate depth separately from final answer quality, otherwise a first-stage miss looks like a reranker failure. Tuning is a sweep: candidate count and final context size against held-out answer quality and end-to-end latency, watching the point where extra candidates stop changing the top results. The gain justifies the latency when relevance is genuinely the bottleneck; if answers fail because the corpus lacks the fact, reranking buys nothing.

Read: [Contextual Retrieval in AI Systems](https://www.anthropic.com/news/contextual-retrieval)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="rag-citations"></a>47. How would you connect each factual claim in an answer to the retrieved passage that supports it?

*System design · [RAG and retrieval](../themes/rag-retrieval.md) · [Checklist](../themes/rag-retrieval.md#rag-citations)*

The point is that attaching a source is not evidence of support, so I design for claim-level attribution and then verify it. Generation emits each factual sentence with the identifier of the passage it used, ideally with character offsets, which keeps the binding checkable instead of a bibliography appended at the end. A separate verification step then asks whether the cited passage actually entails the claim — an entailment model or a second-pass judge, calibrated against a human-labelled sample, because a judge that rubber-stamps is worse than no check. Claims that fail get dropped, marked unsupported, or trigger abstention, and I measure the share of sentences with a verified citation, precision of citations on a labelled set, and how often the system abstains. The limit is that entailment only proves the passage says it; if retrieval surfaced a stale document, a perfectly supported claim can still be false.

Read: [Patterns for Building LLM-based Systems & Products](https://eugeneyan.com/writing/llm-patterns/)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="agt-mcp"></a>48. What does MCP standardise between an AI application and an external service that a model's function-call format does not?

*Knowledge · [Agents, tools and protocols](../themes/agents-tools.md) · [Checklist](../themes/agents-tools.md#agt-mcp)*

A function-call format describes only the shape of the arguments a model emits. It says nothing about where the tool lives, how the application learns the tool exists, or how the result comes back. MCP standardises that surrounding layer — a client-server handshake, capability discovery, and typed primitives for tools, resources and prompts over a defined transport — so the same server works with any compliant application, within the capabilities both sides declare at the handshake, and a tool can be added without changing the model or redeploying the client. Execution and authority stay outside the model: the host application still decides which servers are connected and what each may do. I would judge it by how much integration code disappears per new tool. The trade-off is the trust boundary it creates: a connected server contributes tool descriptions and returns content, both of which reach the context as untrusted input, so a third-party server is a supply-chain and prompt-injection surface.

Read: [Model Context Protocol specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification) · [Security Best Practices](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/2026-07-28/tutorials/security/security_best_practices)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="agt-memory"></a>49. Design memory for an agent that works across many sessions: what is persisted, retrieved, revised and forgotten?

*System design · [Agents, tools and protocols](../themes/agents-tools.md) · [Checklist](../themes/agents-tools.md#agt-memory)*

I'd keep two stores with different lifecycles: the session's working context, filled and discarded, and durable memory, where only confirmed things graduate: stable preferences, decisions with their rationale, task outcomes. The real choice is what gets written. I extract at write time into structured records, subject, attribute, value, source and timestamp, rather than embedding raw transcripts, because a keyed record can be superseded when the user changes their mind, while two contradictory transcript chunks both stay retrievable. The cost is lost detail, so raw episodes are kept briefly as a fallback, not as memory. Retrieval returns a handful of records relevant to the current task, never the whole history, which would recreate the context problem. Forgetting is explicit: expiry for time-bound facts, supersession by key, deletion on request. I'd replay multi-session tasks with memory off and on, measuring success, the share of recalled records actually used and errors caused by stale ones. The boundary: memory the model inferred rather than was told reinforces its own mistakes, so inferences get lower trust or aren't stored.

Read: [Effective context engineering for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="agt-multi-agent"></a>50. When does splitting work among agents improve results, and when do coordination costs dominate?

*Knowledge · [Agents, tools and protocols](../themes/agents-tools.md) · [Checklist](../themes/agents-tools.md#agt-multi-agent)*

Splitting helps when the work genuinely decomposes: subtasks that can run without seeing each other's intermediate state, and whose results a synthesis step can combine — broad search over many sources is the clean case, because breadth is parallel and each branch is independent. It stops helping when agents must agree as they go. Every handoff is a lossy summary through natural language, so shared mutable state produces conflicting edits, duplicated effort and contradictory findings that someone has to reconcile. I would define delegation boundaries and completion criteria per subagent, then make synthesis an explicit step that surfaces disagreement rather than averaging it away. The honest comparison is against one agent given the same total token budget, counting duplicate work, coordination failures, cost and wall-clock latency. Multi-agent often wins latency and loses cost, and if a task is inherently sequential, coordination overhead is pure loss.

Read: [How we built our multi-agent research system](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="eval-hallucination"></a>51. How would you measure unsupported claims in a deployed RAG application without treating every fluent answer as correct?

*System design · [Evaluation and observability](../themes/evals-observability.md) · [Checklist](../themes/evals-observability.md#eval-hallucination)*

Fluency is not the signal, so I measure faithfulness against the evidence the system actually retrieved, not against the world. The unit is a claim: decompose the answer into separate statements and label each supported, contradicted or unsupported by the retrieved passages. That judgement scales with an LLM judge, but only after I calibrate it against a human-labelled sample, because an uncalibrated judge inherits the same plausibility bias I am trying to detect. Attribution matters as much as the rate: if the supporting passage was never retrieved, that is a retrieval defect, and improving the prompt will not fix it. On live traffic I would sample by segment rather than uniformly, since failures cluster in thin or ambiguous parts of the corpus. The limit is that a claim faithful to a retrieved passage can still be wrong if the source is stale, so faithfulness measures grounding, not truth.

Read: [Your AI Product Needs Evals](https://hamel.dev/blog/posts/evals/)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="eval-reasoning-trace-faithfulness"></a>52. A reasoning summary looks sound, but the answer follows a misleading hint. What should an evaluation and monitoring system conclude?

*Applied scenario · [Evaluation and observability](../themes/evals-observability.md) · [Checklist](../themes/evals-observability.md#eval-reasoning-trace-faithfulness)*

The conclusion is that the explanation is not evidence about the computation. A summary that reads well while the answer tracks a planted hint tells you the account is unfaithful, not that the model reasoned well and slipped. So the system should score what it can observe — final answers, tool calls, actions taken — independently of how coherent the narration looks, and never let a plausible summary raise confidence in a wrong result. The diagnostic I would build is paired: run otherwise identical tasks with and without the misleading hint, then measure two things separately, how often the answer moves with the hint, and how often the explanation admits the hint influenced it. A wide gap is the faithfulness signal. In monitoring, treat traces and summaries as useful, incomplete hints for triage. They are not a window into hidden reasoning, so a clean trace is not a safety guarantee.

Read: [Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05410)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="sd-model-api"></a>53. Design a secure developer API for model access, including authentication, quotas, streaming responses and backwards compatibility.

*System design · [AI system design](../themes/ai-system-design.md) · [Checklist](../themes/ai-system-design.md#sd-model-api)*

This endpoint is a contract other people build on, so every decision must survive clients I cannot upgrade. Authentication is per key with scopes and rotation; quotas meter tokens and concurrency, not just request counts, because two requests can differ in token cost by orders of magnitude and a long stream holds capacity for its whole duration; a rejection returns remaining budget and a retry hint rather than a bare error. Streaming needs its own contract: incremental events carrying a request id, an explicit terminal event, and defined behaviour when the stream dies mid-answer, since a truncated reply is not safe to retry blindly. Compatibility comes from additive change — new optional fields, versioned model names, deprecation windows backed by usage telemetry. The hard part is that model behaviour is not versionable the way a schema is: identical requests drift over time, so the promise must cover the interface and documented limits, never identical output.

Read: [Scaling your API with rate limiters](https://stripe.com/blog/rate-limiters)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="mm-latency"></a>54. Build an end-to-end latency budget for a voice agent, from detecting the end of speech to playing its reply.

*System design · [Multimodal and voice](../themes/multimodal-voice.md) · [Checklist](../themes/multimodal-voice.md#mm-latency)*

I budget to the first audible sound, because that is what a caller perceives as responsiveness, and I enumerate every stage before it: end-of-turn detection, final transcription, model time to first token, enough text to synthesise a first chunk, synthesis, network transport and client buffering. The least obvious term, and often one of the largest, is turn detection — waiting for silence to be confident the user finished — and it trades directly against interruptions: shorten it and the agent talks over people, lengthen it and the agent feels slow. Streaming is what makes the sum survivable, since transcription, generation and synthesis overlap instead of queueing, so I track each stage's contribution separately and set a median and a p95 target, because the tail is what callers remember. A budget has to hold under load as well, so I also define degradation: a shorter reply, a filler acknowledgement, or a cheaper voice when a stage overruns.

Read: [The Tail at Scale](https://research.google/pubs/the-tail-at-scale/)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="code-agent-loop"></a>55. Implement a minimal agent runner with validated tool dispatch, error handling and a hard step limit.

*Coding · [Practical coding](../themes/coding-practical.md) · [Checklist](../themes/coding-practical.md#code-agent-loop)*

I would make the loop's state an explicit object — message history, step counter, deadline, budget and a termination reason — because state hidden in control flow is what makes a runner hard to stop, test and debug. Each iteration asks the model for one action, and dispatch goes through a registry: resolve the tool by name, reject anything unregistered, validate arguments against its schema, then call it. An unknown tool or bad argument is not a crash but an observation returned to the model so it can correct itself, while genuine infrastructure failures retry under a bounded policy. Termination must be reachable several ways — a final answer, the step limit, the deadline, the budget, an unrecoverable error — and the runner records which one fired. I would test the limit path and an always-failing tool: an agent that cannot stop is the expensive failure. It omits approval for consequential actions and persistence across restarts.

Read: [Building Effective AI Agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="inf-latency-metrics"></a>56. Distinguish time to first token, time per output token, inter-token latency and throughput when comparing serving systems.

*Knowledge · [Inference, serving and cost](../themes/inference-economics.md) · [Checklist](../themes/inference-economics.md#inf-latency-metrics)*

Three of these describe what one user experiences and throughput describes capacity, so under load they pull in opposite directions. Time to first token runs from request arrival to the first token: queueing plus prefill, so it grows with prompt length and queue depth. Time per output token is the average decode pace after that, end-to-end time minus TTFT divided by the remaining tokens. Inter-token latency is that pace as a distribution of individual gaps, exposing stalls an average hides, for example when the scheduler admits a long prefill and every running decode pauses. Throughput is aggregate tokens or requests per second. Larger batches raise throughput and slow each user's decode, so a throughput figure means nothing without the latency it was bought at. I'd compare systems at matched request rate and length distributions, report p50 and p99 for each latency metric, and quote throughput as the highest load still meeting the latency targets. Token counts aren't comparable across tokenisers, and offline batch jobs care only about throughput and cost.

Read: [vLLM documentation](https://docs.vllm.ai/)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="llm-flashattention"></a>57. Why can an exact attention kernel run faster without changing the quadratic attention computation?

*Knowledge · [LLM fundamentals](../themes/llm-fundamentals.md) · [Checklist](../themes/llm-fundamentals.md#llm-flashattention)*

Because on a GPU standard attention is limited by memory traffic, not arithmetic. The usual kernel writes the N-by-N score matrix to high-bandwidth memory, reads it back for the softmax, writes the probabilities, then reads them again to multiply by V. FlashAttention tiles Q, K and V into blocks that fit in on-chip SRAM and keeps a running maximum and sum per row, the online softmax, rescaling the partial output as each key block arrives, so the full matrix never lands in HBM. FLOPs stay quadratic; the backward pass even adds some, recomputing scores from saved softmax statistics rather than storing them, and still wins because far fewer bytes move. It's exact, differing from standard attention only by floating-point summation order, unlike sparse or low-rank methods that change what's computed. I'd benchmark the real sequence lengths, head widths, masking and dtype on the target GPU, checking agreement within tolerance. At short sequences attention isn't the bottleneck, and in single-token decode attention's cost is reading the KV cache, a different problem.

Read: [FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135)

[↑ Contents](#contents)

### <a id="sd-text-to-sql"></a>58. Design natural-language querying over a warehouse with thousands of tables, from schema selection to safe query execution.

*System design · [AI system design](../themes/ai-system-design.md) · [Checklist](../themes/ai-system-design.md#sd-text-to-sql)*

With thousands of tables the hard part is choosing the schema, not writing SQL, and the real risk is a query that runs and returns a wrong number. So I'd retrieve a small candidate set from the catalog, using table and column descriptions, governed metric definitions, known join paths and verified example queries, and generate against that, preferring a semantic layer where metrics like revenue are already defined, because raw joins invite fan-out double counting. Permissions aren't the model's job: the query runs read-only under the requesting user's own warehouse identity, so row and column security apply, after parsing confirms a single SELECT over catalogued objects, with a cost estimate, timeout and row limit. Ambiguity gets a clarifying question, and the answer shows the SQL and its assumptions. I'd evaluate on real questions with verified queries, comparing result sets rather than SQL text, and measure schema-retrieval recall separately, since a missed table caps everything downstream. Where definitions are contested or undocumented, generation can't fix that; curated metrics come first.

Read: [OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications](https://genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10/) · [Spider 2.0: Evaluating Language Models on Real-World Enterprise Text-to-SQL Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.07763)
